title: Implied main ideas and the best title
blurb: Build the main idea when no sentence states it, and choose the title that names the topic and reflects that idea without being too broad or too narrow.
question: A HESI A2 passage describes a school nurse checking a student's blood sugar, screening vision and teaching a hand-washing class, but no sentence sums it up. The question asks: 'Which title best fits the passage?' One choice is 'Health in American Schools'; another is 'Vision Screening for Children'. How do you build the main idea and pick the title?

teach.body: Formally, an implied main idea is the central point a passage makes without stating it in any one sentence; the reader infers it from what the details have in common. A best title names the topic and reflects that main idea. Plain English: the author shows you the pieces and lets you see the picture. Your job is to name the picture, in a sentence for 'main idea' questions and in a short label for 'best title' questions.

steps.label: Common thread?
steps.sub: what do all the gists share

teach.body:
(1) By 8:15 a.m., Ms. Alvarez has already checked a second grader's blood sugar before breakfast, iced a sprained ankle from the playground and called a parent about a rising fever.

(2) Between visits, she screens fourth graders' vision and hearing and updates the records that show which students are missing required vaccines. Twice a week she meets with teachers to plan for a student who has severe food allergies.

(3) On Friday afternoons she visits kindergarten classrooms with a glow-in-the-dark lotion that shows children how much 'germ' is left on their hands after a quick rinse.

teach.h: Gists under the implied main idea

root.label: Implied main idea
root.sub: A school nurse meets a wide range of health needs

teach.caption: No sentence says 'school nurses do far more than first aid', yet every paragraph shows it.

teach.h: Building the main idea in four moves
items: Write a gist for each paragraph: daily care; screening and records; teaching.
Ask what the gists share: one nurse, many kinds of health work.
Draft one sentence that covers all three: 'A school nurse handles a wide range of student health needs.'
Test it: does every paragraph fit under it, and does it claim nothing the passage never shows? If yes, keep it.

teach.body: A title is a short label for the main idea. The best title names the topic AND points to what the passage says about it. It fails if it is too broad (it would fit a whole book), too narrow (it fits one paragraph), off center (catchy but about something else) or inaccurate (it promises something the passage does not deliver, such as a cure or a ranking).

head: Title
Verdict
Why
rows: Fits a book on school health
A Day's Work for a School Nurse
Topic plus the range of work

teach.text: Implied-idea traps: a vivid detail offered as the whole point (the glow lotion); a recommendation the author never makes ('Every school should hire two nurses'); the topic sentence of one paragraph passed off as the whole passage's idea; and a catchy title built on a striking detail. A title can sound good and still be wrong if it covers only part of the passage.

teach.body: Keanu Akana, applying to a radiography program, gets the school nurse passage with four titles. He writes gists in the margin (care, screening, teaching), then tests each title: 'Vision Screening for Children' fits paragraph 2 only; 'Health in American Schools' would fit a textbook; 'Glow Lotion and Germs' is a catchy detail. 'A Day's Work for a School Nurse' covers all three gists, so he picks it in under a minute.

items: An implied main idea is not stated; build it from what every paragraph's gist has in common.
Write a 3-5 word gist per paragraph, then one sentence that covers them all.
The best title names the topic and reflects the main idea.
Reject titles and main ideas that are too broad, too narrow, off center or inaccurate.
Never key a recommendation the author does not make.

summary: You can now build the main idea of a passage that never states it, by writing a gist for each paragraph and finding what they share. You can also choose the best title by checking that it names the topic, reflects the main idea and is neither too broad nor too narrow.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) At 6 a.m., before the first bus leaves the depot, mechanics at the Riverton transit garage test every wheelchair lift.

(2) Drivers on Route 4 now wait an extra minute at the senior center, and the stop outside the dialysis clinic has a new heated shelter.

(3) Last year the city also added a phone line that lets riders book door-to-door trips a day ahead.

Which statement best expresses the implied main idea of the passage about Riverton's buses?
options: Riverton is making its buses easier for riders with health needs.
Mechanics test every wheelchair lift before the first bus leaves.
Public transit is the most important service a city can provide.
Riverton plans to replace its bus routes with door-to-door trips.
A.why: Each paragraph shows a change that helps riders with health or mobility needs: lift checks, extra time and a shelter, and door-to-door booking. No sentence states it, but every detail fits under it.

whyNot.1: Too narrow: this is the detail from paragraph 1.
whyNot.2: Too broad and unsupported: the passage never compares city services.
whyNot.3: Unsupported: the phone line adds door-to-door trips; nothing says routes will be replaced.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Canker sores and cold sores are often confused, but they differ in more than name. Canker sores are small, shallow ulcers that form inside the mouth, on the gums or inner cheeks. They are not contagious, and their exact cause is not fully understood.

(2) Cold sores, by contrast, are clusters of tiny blisters that usually appear on or around the lips. They are caused by a herpes simplex virus and can spread through close contact, such as kissing or sharing a cup.

Which title best fits the passage about mouth sores?
options: Why Cold Sores Spread Through Close Contact
Common Problems of the Mouth and Teeth
Canker Sores and Cold Sores: How They Differ
How to Heal a Canker Sore Overnight
A.why: The passage contrasts the two sores (location, cause, contagiousness). The title names both and the point that they differ.

whyNot.0: Too narrow: contagion is one detail about cold sores in paragraph 2.
whyNot.1: Too broad: the passage covers two kinds of sore, not mouth and tooth problems in general.
whyNot.3: Inaccurate: the passage gives no treatment, let alone an overnight cure.

A.q: A passage's three paragraphs describe a hospital's new rooftop garden, patients who say time there eases their stress, and nurses who use it for short breaks. No sentence sums them up. What should a reader do to find the main idea?
options: Choose the first sentence, which introduces the garden
Choose the detail that seems most vivid or memorable
Choose the last sentence, because it ends the passage
Combine the paragraph points into one covering idea
A.why: With no stated main idea, the reader builds one: write what each paragraph shows (a garden, calmer patients, rested nurses) and find the idea that covers all three.

whyNot.0: The first sentence introduces the topic, but here it covers paragraph 1 only.
whyNot.1: A vivid detail is the classic too-narrow trap.
whyNot.2: Position alone does not make a sentence the main idea, and here no sentence sums up the passage.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) In the 1840s, Dr. Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that far more new mothers died of fever on a Vienna hospital ward staffed by doctors and medical students than on a ward run by midwives.

(2) The students often came to the ward directly from performing autopsies.

(3) When Semmelweis required everyone to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients, deaths on the doctors' ward fell sharply.

Which statement best expresses the implied main idea of the passage about Semmelweis?
options: Midwives of the 1840s were better trained than doctors were.
Semmelweis showed that hand washing could prevent many deaths.
Medical students of the 1840s often performed autopsies.
Chlorine is the most effective cleaner for a hospital ward.
B.why: The details form a chain: more deaths where students came from autopsies, then a sharp drop once everyone washed in chlorine. Together they imply that hand washing prevented many deaths.

whyNot.0: Unsupported: the passage compares death rates, not training.
whyNot.2: Too narrow: this is the single detail in paragraph 2.
whyNot.3: Overstatement: the passage says chlorine washing helped, not that chlorine is the best cleaner.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) A service dog is trained to perform specific tasks for a person with a disability. One dog may alert its owner to an oncoming seizure; another may guide a person who is blind across a busy street.

(2) An emotional support animal, by contrast, comforts its owner simply by being present and needs no special task training. Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, stores and restaurants must admit service dogs but are not required to admit emotional support animals.

Which title best fits the passage about assistance animals?
options: How Service Dogs Sense an Oncoming Seizure
The Many Ways Animals Improve Our Health
Why Stores Should Welcome Every Animal
Service Dogs and Support Animals Compared
B.why: The passage contrasts the two kinds of animal in training, role and legal access. The title names both and signals the comparison.

whyNot.0: Too narrow and inaccurate: seizure alerts are one example, and the passage never explains how dogs sense them.
whyNot.1: Too broad: the passage covers two kinds of assistance animal, not animals and health in general.
whyNot.2: Off center and unsupported: the author takes no position, and the law described does not require stores to admit every animal.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Jordan had worked as an emergency medical technician for six years when he applied to nursing school.

(2) On calls, he had learned to stay calm while a family shouted questions. He could take a blood pressure in a moving ambulance and explain a procedure in words a frightened child understood. He had also watched patients he handed off in the ER improve under the care of nurses he admired.

What is the implied main idea of paragraph 2 of the passage about Jordan?
options: Jordan's EMT years had readied him for nursing and drawn him to it.
Jordan could take a blood pressure reading in a moving ambulance.
Emergency medical technicians earn less money than nurses earn.
Families of patients often shout questions at emergency workers.
B.why: The skills he gained (calm, clinical skill, clear explanation) and the nurses he admired together imply that his EMT work prepared him for nursing and attracted him to it.

whyNot.1: Too narrow: one skill among several.
whyNot.2: Outside knowledge: pay is never mentioned.
whyNot.3: Too narrow and overgeneralized: one situation from Jordan's calls, stated as a general rule.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Unlike a tetanus shot, which protects for about ten years, the flu vaccine is recommended every year. The reason lies in the virus itself.

(2) Influenza viruses change constantly. Small changes in their surface proteins can make last year's antibodies less able to recognize this year's strains. Protection from a flu shot also fades over the months after vaccination.

(3) Each winter, scientists study which strains are spreading around the world and predict which are likely to dominate the next season. Manufacturers then need about six months to produce the new vaccine, which is why the choice is made long before flu season begins.

Which title best fits the passage about the flu vaccine?
options: How Manufacturers Make a Vaccine in Six Months
The Long History of the Influenza Virus
Why a New Flu Vaccine Is Needed Each Year
Why a Tetanus Shot Lasts About Ten Years
C.why: Paragraph 1 raises the question (why every year?), paragraph 2 gives the virus's reasons and paragraph 3 explains how each year's vaccine is chosen. The title covers all three.

whyNot.0: Too narrow: production time is one detail in paragraph 3, and the passage does not explain how vaccines are made.
whyNot.1: Off center: the passage explains yearly vaccination, not the virus's history.
whyNot.3: Off center: tetanus is a comparison in the first sentence, not the subject.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) For two centuries, lighthouse keepers climbed winding stairs each night to trim wicks and polish lenses along the American coast. By the late twentieth century, automated lamps had replaced nearly all of them.

(2) Satellite navigation now guides most ships, yet many lighthouses still shine, maintained by the Coast Guard as backups. Others have been sold or leased to towns and nonprofit groups, which run them as museums, inns and wedding sites.

(3) In some coastal towns, volunteers spend weekends repainting towers and leading tours for visitors who climb the same stairs the keepers once did.

Which statement best expresses the implied main idea of the passage about lighthouses?
options: Satellite navigation has made lighthouses useless to ships.
Lighthouses have lost their keepers but found new roles.
Volunteers repaint lighthouse towers on summer weekends.
Lighthouse keepers had some of the hardest jobs in America.
C.why: Paragraph 1 shows the keepers disappearing; paragraphs 2 and 3 show lighthouses serving as backups, museums, inns and volunteer-run sites. The covering idea: keepers are gone, but the lighthouses have new roles.

whyNot.0: Contradiction: many lighthouses are maintained as backups for ships.
whyNot.2: Too narrow, and 'summer' is not in the passage.
whyNot.3: Outside the passage: it never ranks the difficulty of keepers' work.

C.q: The implied main idea of a passage is: 'Small changes at home can cut a family's water use without much effort.' Which title best fits that passage?
options: Easy Ways to Save Water at Home
Water Use in the Modern World
Fixing a Leaky Faucet in Ten Minutes
The Global Fight Over Fresh Water
C.why: The title names the topic (water use at home) and reflects the point (small, easy changes save water).

whyNot.1: Too broad: the passage is about one family's home, not the modern world.
whyNot.2: Too narrow: one possible change, not the passage's whole point.
whyNot.3: Off topic: the passage is about home habits, not global conflict.

reteach.title: A puzzle without the box
reteach.question: Someone hands you a bag of puzzle pieces with no picture on the box. How do you work out what the picture is, and what would you write on the box lid?

blocks.body: You sort the pieces by what they show (sky, sand, a striped umbrella), then ask what single scene includes all of them: a day at the beach. That scene is the implied main idea. The label you write on the lid is the title: 'A Day at the Beach' fits; 'Umbrellas' is one piece (too narrow); 'Summer' could be a thousand puzzles (too broad).

blocks.text: The brightest piece is not the picture. A title or main idea built on the most eye-catching detail is the classic too-narrow answer.

explain.body: Write 3-5 words for what each paragraph shows. Then look for the idea that all the gists share. That shared idea, written as a full sentence, is the implied main idea.

test.q: A student writes these gists for a three-paragraph passage: (1) a clinic now stays open until 9 p.m.; (2) it has added Saturday hours; (3) it offers video visits. Which implied main idea covers all three?
options: The clinic now stays open until 9 p.m. on weekdays.
Video visits are replacing in-person visits to clinics.
The clinic has made care easier to fit into busy lives.
Clinics should offer Saturday hours to every patient.
test.why: Late hours, Saturday hours and video visits all make care easier to reach around work and family schedules.

whyNot.0: Too narrow: this is gist 1 only.
whyNot.1: Unsupported and too broad: the clinic added video visits; nothing says they replace in-person care anywhere.
whyNot.3: A recommendation the passage does not make.

explain.body: If one sentence covers every paragraph, the main idea is stated. If each paragraph makes its own point and none sums up the whole, the main idea is implied, and you must build it.

test.q: Which feature of a passage best signals that its main idea is implied rather than stated?
options: The first sentence asks the reader a question
Several paragraphs include numbers and dates
The final paragraph offers advice to readers
No single sentence sums up every paragraph
test.why: An implied main idea is one that no sentence states, so the signal is the absence of a sentence covering the whole passage.

whyNot.0: A hook question often comes before a stated main idea; it does not show the idea is implied.
whyNot.1: Numbers and dates are supporting details; they say nothing about whether the main idea is stated.
whyNot.2: Advice may itself state the author's main point, so it does not signal an implied idea.

explain.body: A title names the topic and reflects the main idea in a few words. Test each choice: does it cover every paragraph (not too narrow), stay inside the passage (not too broad) and promise only what the passage delivers?

head: Check
Fails if
rows: It promises a cure or ranking

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Ticks are most active from spring through early fall, when hikers are most likely to meet them.

(2) Hikers can lower their risk by staying on cleared trails, wearing long sleeves and using insect repellent. After a hike, a careful check of the skin, scalp and clothing can catch ticks before they stay attached for long.

Which title best fits the passage about ticks?
options: Avoiding Tick Bites on the Trail
When Ticks Are Most Active
Insects and Human Disease
Choosing an Insect Repellent
test.why: The passage tells hikers when ticks are out and how to avoid bites. The title names the topic and the point.

whyNot.1: Too narrow: the season is the opening detail in paragraph 1.
whyNot.2: Too broad: the passage covers one pest and how to avoid it.
whyNot.3: Too narrow: repellent is one of several steps.

explain.body: Reject choices that add a recommendation the author never makes, focus on one measure or detail, or reach beyond the passage. The right implied main idea is the most modest statement that still covers everything.

test.q: A passage describes how three hospitals cut patient falls with bed alarms, nonslip socks and hourly rounding. Why is 'Every hospital must install bed alarms' a poor statement of its implied main idea?
options: It names the topic but leaves out the author's point
It adds a demand and centers on one of three measures
It is broader than the passage, covering all of health care
It repeats a sentence stated word for word in the passage
test.why: The passage reports what three hospitals did; it does not demand anything, and bed alarms are only one of the three measures.

whyNot.0: The statement makes a claim, so it is not a bare topic; the problem is the added demand and narrow focus.
whyNot.2: It is narrow, not broad: it centers on one measure in hospitals.
whyNot.3: Nothing indicates the passage contains this sentence; it adds a demand the passage does not make.
